html:
The flight of French Protestants, the Huguenots, after Louis XIV outlawed their faith in 1685. Some 200,000 left France in the years that followed, though leaving was itself forbidden.

Since the Edict of Nantes of 1598, Huguenots had been allowed to worship in set places. Louis wanted one king, one faith. From 1681 soldiers were billeted in Protestant homes to bully families into converting, the dragonnades. In October 1685 the Edict of Fontainebleau revoked Nantes, closed Protestant churches and ordered pastors out.

The refugees went to the Dutch Republic, England, Switzerland and German states. The Elector of Brandenburg invited them with the Edict of Potsdam, and they made up a large share of Berlin's people around 1700, helping build Prussia. Others went to the American colonies and to South Africa (Huguenots at the Cape).

Many were skilled weavers, silk workers, watchmakers and merchants, so France lost trades and capital to its rivals. The English word "refugee" comes from the French name for them.
